newsitem.title: INDIA: Regional leader is front-runner for India PM post.
newsitem.headline: Regional leader is front-runner for India PM post.

text.p: A southern politician close to the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty emerged on Wednesday as a front-runner to become India's next prime minister.

G.K. Moopanar, who defected from the Congress party last year to form a regional party in Tamil Nadu state, appeared well placed ahead of a meeting of the United Front coalition's Steering Committee set for 3:00 p.m. (0930 GMT) on Thursday.
"Moopanar Frontrunner," the Pioneer daily said. "Moopanar leads the race for PM's slot," said the Hindustan Times.

Moopanar was joined by a long list of hopefuls and was by no means assured of being picked to succeed caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, especially as the regional politician had his detractors within the 15-party United Front coalition.
As a former Congress member, Moopanar is seen as a link between the United Front and Congress. He is close to Sonia Gandhi, the widow of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi.
"Is Mrs Sonia Gandhi in politics? She belongs to the Nehru family and it is also a fact that I have worked under Mrs Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi," Moopanar was quoted as saying.
Some faulted Moopanar for lack of experience in governance, and he was said to be opposed by the leader of Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party, Laloo Prasad Yadav, himself a candidate.
Deve Gowda resigned last Friday after losing a vote of confidence in parliament's lower house and was asked to stay on as caretaker prime minister until a new government was formed.
The crisis was triggered when the Congress party decided to withdraw its vital support for his government on March 30.
Since the vote the United Front and Congress, impelled by a common fear of the rightwing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), have tried to sink their differences.

Their apprehension was underlined by a nationwide survey conducted between April 2 and 8 by ORG-Marg which showed that if general elections were held now, the Hindu nationalist BJP and its four allies would win 237 to 253 seats in the 542-member lower house of parliament, up from 193 now and within striking distance of an absolute majority.
The United Front's total would fall to 150 to 164 seats from its current total of 178, while Congress would manage only 112 to 126 seats, down from 140, the survey said.

On Sunday, Deve Gowda offered to step down as United Front leader, meeting Congress's main condition for renewing support. Congress announced on Monday that it would back any United Front leader other than Deve Gowda for the prime minister's post.
But hurdles remained on the path to a new government.

The BJP wrote to President Sharma on Tuesday, saying it would be "unprecedented, unethical and unacceptable" for the president to invite the same coalition which lost a vote of confidence to form a fresh government.

The Hindu party also said all efforts should be exhausted to form a new government before parliament takes up the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, which has delighted investors but been held hostage by the 18-day political crisis.
Parliament was set to take up the budget on April 21, but it was not clear whether the special three-day session would go ahead if the United Front agreed on a new leader before then.
The two communist parties in the United Front have also voiced doubts about the budget and want Congress to withdraw a formal claim to power before the alliance names a new chief.
